newsitem.title: ITALY: Food summit security set to give Rome indigestion.
newsitem.headline: Food summit security set to give Rome indigestion.

text.p: More armed men will be on the streets of Rome than at any time since the city's liberation in World War Two when some 100 heads of state and government fly in this week for a global food summit.

Roads will be closed, a ring of steel will be erected around the venue and police cars with lights flashing will whisk leaders to and from the World Food Summit while ordinary Romans curse the extra congestion in their already chaotic city.
"It's going to be a nightmare," said one Italian official who hoped to keep out of the way for the five-day meeting, which opens on Wednesday.
A senior official at the police headquarters in Rome said some 10,000 police and paramilitary Carabinieri would be deployed, many of them drafted in from other parts of Italy.

They will mount a 24-hour guard of the headquarters of the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation, the summit venue. More than 10,000 delegates, officials from non-governmental organisations and journalists are expected for the event.
Police will be stationed outside more than 70 hotels and at ambassadors' residences where an estimated 170 VIPs will stay.
Even though Rome staged the Olympic Games in 1960 and the World Cup in 1990, the challenges of looking after more than half the world's leaders for a week is monumental.
Cuban President Fidel Castro, whose island is one of communism's last bastions, is among those expected to attend, though FAO has so far withheld names on security grounds.
Castro and Pope John Paul, who will open the gathering, will be among those most closely watched.
"It's a security operation on an unprecedented scale," said the police official, who declined to be identified.
He said many of the individual countries' own security squads were already in Rome and were liaising with police.
For people living and working around FAO headquarters near ancient Rome's Circus Maximus racetrack, the Colosseum and other landmarks of The Eternal City, the week promises to be hell.

The summit site, a Fascist-era building close to the gateway through which Allied forces entered in June 1944 to free Rome from Nazi German occupation, lies on one of the city's busiest thoroughfares, which will be closed to traffic.
The capital's cobbled streets are already clogged with too many cars, thousands of motor scooters and by the disruptions of road works begun during the summer but not yet finished.
Police recognise that residents will "probably have some difficulties" as all roads around FAO and the nearest metro station are sealed off and sniffer dogs and bomb squads move in.
Residents and shopkeepers in the area must show their identity cards just to be allowed to go to work or come home.
FAO staff not involved in the summit say they have been told to go on holiday or work from home for the week. The sports ground, soon to become a helicopter pad, is already closed.
Apart from delegates, only 4,000 accredited journalists and key FAO personnel, wearing special identity badges, will be allowed inside the building, where 500 police will be on duty.
Inside, there will be metal detectors and special containers for the leaders' own bodyguards to deposit their guns if they have not already disposed of them, a senior Carabinieri officer said.
But one headache has been removed. Italy's metalworkers had planned to hold a national demonstration in Rome next Friday to press for more pay but have rescheduled the protest.
